primary.title: US: Jets clip wings at Reagan National Airport
primary.description: Two American Airlines Boeing 737-800 aircraft clipped each other's wings while taxiing for departure at Ronald Reagan Washington National Airport on Friday, prompting an emergency response and an investigation by the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA).The collision occurred around 5.10 pm local time when Flight 638, bound for Dallas-Fort Worth, made contact with Flight 2152, which was scheduled to fly to Chicago's O'Hare International Airport. Neither aircraft had taken off, and no injuries were reported.Also read | US begins cleanup as holiday floods and storms ease; 360,000 remain without powerBoth aircraft returned to their gates and were withdrawn from service for maintenance inspections. American Airlines is arranging alternative aircraft to carry passengers to their destinations.The incident comes amid growing scrutiny of aviation safety and operational reliability in the US, where technology failures, air traffic control disruptions and airport incidents have repeatedly interrupted air travel in recent months.The Reagan National incident is the latest in a string of problems confronting US air travel.Earlier this month, a communications failure in the FAA's air traffic control network triggered a nationwide ground stop lasting more than four hours.The disruption affected more than 18,000 flights and 1.5 million passengers, according to Reuters. The failure exposed vulnerabilities in an ageing communications infrastructure that the government has been trying to modernise.The FAA's network has also faced problems from damaged telecommunications cables, outdated equipment and failures involving backup systems.In September, a communications failure at a Philadelphia air traffic facility, compounded by the accidental cutting of a backup fibre-optic cable in New Jersey, disrupted around 9,500 flights.Also read | US Black Friday online sales to cross $13 billion, Adobe saysAirports have faced equipment failures as well. On November 24, a ground surveillance radar outage at Chicago O'Hare disrupted arrivals, with delays averaging 47 minutes and some aircraft forced to hold in the air.The system monitors aircraft and vehicles on runways and taxiways, making it a critical part of airport operations.Airline technology has added to the disruptions. A malfunction in Delta Air Lines' automated aircraft weight-calculation system delayed more than 1,000 flights ahead of Thanksgiving, forcing the carrier to temporarily resort to manual procedures.The incidents have intensified calls for a faster overhaul of America's air traffic control infrastructure.The Trump administration is seeking $50 billion for aviation and airport modernisation, while Congress had already approved $12.5 billion for upgrades in 2025.However, funding is only part of the challenge.The FAA must replace ageing systems while keeping the existing network operational, a complicated process that raises the risk of further disruptions during the transition.The latest collision adds to a growing list of incidents putting the spotlight on US aviation infra.
